questions.prompt: Draw an outline map of Brazil. On it, show and name a feature of relief, the course of a river, two urban centres and an agricultural region.
questions.model: Draw the outline of Brazil with a broad northern bulge across the Amazon, an eastward shoulder at the Northeast, then the coast running south-west and the country tapering to the south. Relief: outline the Brazilian Highlands as an area in the east-centre of the country, inland from the coast, running from the Northeast down to the south, and label it Brazilian Highlands. River: draw the Amazon as a line entering Brazil in the far west and flowing east past Manaus, where the Rio Negro joins from the north-west, to the Atlantic at a wide estuary close to the equator, and mark Marajó Island at the mouth. Urban centres: put a dot for São Paulo inland, just behind the south-east coast near the Tropic of Capricorn, and a dot for Rio de Janeiro on the coast, east-north-east of São Paulo, and name both. questions.prompt: Examine how two factors have influenced the development of secondary economic activity in Brazil.
questions.model: Raw materials and energy. Brazil's industry grew where its raw materials were. Iron ore from Minas Gerais and Carajás feeds steel, and the CSN steelworks at Volta Redonda began production in 1946. Carajás in Pará is the world's largest iron-ore mine, and its ore goes by railway to São Luís for export. Sugar cane is turned into ethanol, so cane in São Paulo state supports a fuel industry. Soya and meat supply food processing, such as JBS. Hydroelectricity from Itaipu, on the Paraná and shared with Paraguay, supplies the Southeast industrial core with cheap power. Tucuruí, on the Tocantins, powers aluminium smelting in the Amazon. Together these resources explain why industry clusters in the Southeast. Government policy. From the 1930s Getúlio Vargas used import substitution industrialisation, protecting factories with tariffs and building heavy industry such as the CSN steelworks and Petrobras. Under Juscelino Kubitschek (1956 to 1961) foreign car makers were invited into the ABC region near São Paulo, and Volkswagen's São Bernardo plant opened in 1959. The Manaus Free Trade Zone (1967) used tax breaks to bring electronics and motorbike assembly to the Amazon. SUDENE (1959) gave incentives to the Northeast, leading to the Camaçari petrochemical complex in Bahia. The Real Plan (1994) ended hyperinflation, and privatisation of Embraer in 1994 and Vale in 1997 opened the economy. The effect was a concentrated industrial triangle of São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Belo Horizonte, with smaller clusters at Manaus and in the Northeast.

questions.prompt: Account for the distribution of population in Brazil.
questions.model: Brazil's overall density is low, about 24 people per km² (2022 Census), because the population of about 203 million is very unevenly spread. The 2022 Census shows the Southeast has about 42 percent of the population, the Northeast about 27 percent, the South about 15 percent, the North about 8.5 percent and the Centre-West about 8 percent. The North covers about 45 percent of the area but holds only about 8.5 percent of the people. Dense areas first. The Southeast is densest, because the plateau climate is cooler than the coast and fertile terra roxa from basalt supported the coffee boom. Its industrial jobs in São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Belo Horizonte, and its services, keep drawing migrants, so São Paulo state has about 44 million people. The coast is dense because colonial settlement came from the sea, with ports such as Santos and Salvador. On the Northeast sugar coast, the Zona da Mata, fertile massapê soils and reliable rain from the trade winds supported plantations that needed large workforces. Cities such as São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Salvador and Fortaleza are dense because they offer jobs and services; the urban share has risen from about 36 percent in 1950 to about 87 percent. Now the sparse areas. The Amazon is sparse because of dense forest that is hard to clear, heat and humidity, disease, poor access and leached latosol soils that fail quickly once cleared. The Centre-West was thinly settled because it was isolated, far from the coast and with few roads, before Brasília was built in 1960. The sertão is sparse because semi-arid rainfall of roughly 250 to 800 mm varies year to year, droughts destroy crops and the soils are thin and stony, so many people left. The contrast is clear: São Paulo state has about 180 people per km² while Amazonas has under 3. Governments tried to move people inland. Brasília was inaugurated on 21 April 1960, the March to the West opened the interior, and the Trans-Amazonian Highway (1970s) and settlement of Rondônia along the BR-364 (1980s) tried to settle the Amazon. Many schemes failed because of poor soils and distance from markets, so the coast and the Southeast still hold most people.
